Product rules — the decisions every feature is held to

The product decisions SATOM's code, documentation and reviews hold to — how a device is written to, why HTTP 200 is not success, why every field is visible, where a page belongs (Settings or Operations), plugins versus basic elements, Plugin Studio, menu folders and the single product language.

These are the product decisions that code, documentation and reviews hold to. Each rule says what it is, why it exists, and — where one exists — the test that enforces it. When a rule changes, this file changes in the same commit.

Related: the team's day-to-day conventions are in Security model, the visual rules in Design system, the hard-won implementation gotchas in Architecture §13, and the architecture vocabulary in NAF framework.

1. Talking to appliances#

1.1 The cache first, the device last#

Presentation reads what the collectors stored. Going to the appliance is an explicit action, run as a job and visible to the operator — never a side effect of opening a page. Day-to-day browsing must not hammer the fleet.

1.2 Writing to a device is six steps#

Every new or reworked write flow (policy clone, mass deploy, provisioning, restore) runs:

  1. Pre-check — reachable, build, licence, HA role (write to the primary).
  2. Versioned backup of what is about to change.
  3. Dry-run diff of intent against the device's actual state.
  4. Minimal change in dependency order — certificate → health check → real server → pool → virtual server / server policy; deletions in reverse order.
  5. Post-check by re-reading the object. FortiWeb silently ignores fields of a PUT; only a re-read catches it.
  6. Compensation or restore with a clear message if anything failed.

A flow is idempotent: the second run makes zero changes. An existing flow that lacks a step is a defect.

1.3 Truth per build, not from memory#

Paths, fields and authentication change between firmware builds. The answer comes from the API library for the exact build, a measurement in the lab, or the vendor documentation for that version. What is not verified is marked — # TODO verify: <product> <build> <endpoint> in code, "unverified on this build" in the interface.

1.4 HTTP 200 is not success#

Read the body. Appliances answer 200 with {"payload": "Invalid VM License"}, licence errors, or their own error codes inside results. A licence failure, a rejected read or a collector that is down is shown as an ERROR — never as empty and never as "ok". A failed metrics collector writes satom_scrape_up 0: absence is not health.

1.5 Everything done to a device leaves a trace#

Every action SATOM takes against an appliance is a step in a job and a line in the audit log. A channel that talks to a device without going through job progress (a login, a GUI reader) is a defect.

1.6 Every field the device has is visible#

In every form of every product (FortiGate, FortiWeb, FortiADC, FortiAnalyzer, FortiAuthenticator), each field of the exact build is shown. What the vendor's GUI shows sits in its section; what it does not show sits in "Not in GUI, but in CLI", with its channel (REST, or CLI through the CLI writer). A field whose channel is unknown says "unverified on this build". Nothing is hidden; without a measured layout the section says so. Implemented in app/services/not_in_gui.py; enforced by tests/test_not_in_gui.py.

2. Security#

  • No secret in code, logs, commits, job steps or output. Credentials are encrypted in the database; keys live in the environment file.
  • TLS is verified by default against the trust store. Verification is off only when an operator turned it off explicitly — never as a fallback.
  • Readers cannot write, by construction. Read-only and read-write device profiles are separate; read paths call assert_readonly.
  • Sessions log out, requests time out, dependencies are pinned.
  • RBAC on the route, not only on the template: hiding a button is not authorisation.
  • Behind a reverse proxy on a non-standard port, the proxy must pass Host $http_host (the installer writes it). Never lower WTF_CSRF_SSL_STRICT to work around a header problem.

3. Architecture: do not mix the blocks#

SATOM maps onto the NAF reference model. A change names the block it touches and does not blur them:

Block In SATOM
Intent Templates, system profiles, processes, the local source of truth
Executor REST writes, the CLI writer
Collector Device sync, the knowledge harvester, metrics collection
Observability Metrics store, drift, CVE/PSIRT
Orchestrator Processes, scheduler, jobs
Presentation Web console, satom CLI, API v1

Signs of mixing: a view that calls the device, a process that writes without intent, a collector that writes.

4. Navigation and information architecture#

4.1 Settings configures; Operations operates#

Decided per card, not per page. A card that writes a value or row that changes behaviour belongs in Settings. State, health, logs, explanations, demos, live lists and one-off actions (sync, list/release) belong in Operations. Example: Settings › AI › Sentinel holds only the Sentinel form, context and response policy; Operations › Sentinel holds the incidents console, overview, border blocklist and architecture. Enforced by tests/test_settings_nav_groups.py.

4.2 A basic element is native; a plugin is a plugin#

A basic element of an ADOM lives natively in that ADOM's menu and can be switched off per ADOM with a capability (for example the Web Server Manager of the Linux ADOM, cap_webserver). What is delivered as a plugin ships as signed plugin packages (several = a bundle). A basic element may also have a bundle for automation (fine-grained steps on the same code) without a menu folder. Never switch off something operators use in the name of unifying it.

4.3 Troubleshooting is a set of plugin apps#

Backend Reachability, Config Compare, HTTP Observatory, Path Diagnostics, Transaction Tracer and Diagnose Log Collection are signed plugin apps in the Troubleshooting menu group; each is one SATOM step over the same code as its page (app/services/studio_troubleshoot.py). There is no native Troubleshooting submenu; the pages remain reachable by URL. A change to one of those pages is reflected in its step.

4.4 In Plugin Studio everything is an app#

  • Two kinds: flow (form + diagram) and script. A script's code stays under data/scripts/, because the sandbox runner must never hold a database connection.
  • Examples are templates and cannot be deleted — by no route (app, script, store, connection). They can be edited, disabled, reset and downloaded.
  • Reset deletes the app's data (its runs and the store rows only that app uses); shared stores are respected.
  • A plugin's code is its dependency, not a second plugin (2026-11-13). A script that a flow app runs is listed under Plugin Studio › Code with the apps that run it and the package that brought it, and in the app's Dependencies tab; it has no row under Apps and no entry under Plugins. A script no app runs is an app of its own. The plugin's logic stays in the plugin (its view or its own scripts); SATOM only gains generic capabilities.
  • A File field takes at most 20 MiB (2026-11-13), the same number for flow apps, scripts and the browser; only an app with a File field takes a run request that large, every other request stays at 1 MiB.

4.5 Menu groups are assigned in SATOM, never in the Builder#

The Builder creates apps; the menu group is assigned in SATOM. Groups are folders: a folder grants its ADOMs and user groups to all its apps, adding to each app's own grants, never removing. A folder is chosen from a list ("+ New folder…"), never typed as free text. A package carries the folder name only — never the grants.

4.6 Top-level entries#

Plugin Studio is a first-level sidebar entry. Scout sits directly above Wiki.

5. Language#

Everything the product ships is English: the interface, installers and builders, deployment scripts, --help text, generated file headers, code comments, documentation, the changelog and tests. One language — no --lang, no LANG detection, no fallback. Requests quoted in the changelog are quoted translated.

Exceptions: the web console's translations (German, Spanish, French, Italian through Babel; English is the default), language names, app/translations/, internationalisation test fixtures, and installers silently accepting s/si as yes for answer files written by old versions.

Measure compliance with a stop-word scorer, not with a grep for accented letters: most non-English text is plain ASCII.

6. Look and feel#

SATOM is a light product built on its own tokens and components. The full rules — stylesheets, colours, badges, card grids, charts, plugin views — are in Design system.

7. Documentation and tests travel with the change#

  • A change with visible behaviour updates, in the same round, the user guide, the CHANGELOG.md entry and the matching Documentation Center article.
  • A new or changed test runs targeted; only a green test lands on main. The full suite runs nightly against main.
  • Only the test files of the touched modules run during development; the full suite is not a per-change ritual.

8. Licence#

SATOM is licensed under the Elastic License 2.0: source-available, free for internal use including production; offering it to third parties as a hosted or managed service needs a commercial licence (see LICENSE). Eight surfaces declare the licence and must agree — tests/test_license_consistency.py.
